# Introduction

This analysis examines changes in Italian government bond yields
using a three-state Gaussian Hidden Markov Model. The model allows
the mean and variance of nominal yields to depend on an unobserved
state, with transitions governed by a Markov chain.

We estimate the model using monthly observations from January 1997
to July 2019 and decode the most likely state sequence. States are
labelled by their estimated mean yields rather than interpreted
automatically as economic expansions or crises.

# Data and Exploratory Analysis

The dataset contains 271 monthly observations on nominal 10-year
Italian government bond yields, inflation, and additional
macroeconomic and credit-rating variables. The HMM uses nominal
yields only.

For descriptive comparison, we also display nominal yields minus
contemporaneous inflation. This is an approximate inflation-adjusted
measure, rather than an ex ante real yield based on expected inflation.

```{r data-import, include=FALSE}
data_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
  "MnGianmaria/time-series-analysis/main/",
  "03_hidden_markov_models/data/",
  "italian_bond_yields.csv"
)

df <- read.csv(data_url)

df$Date <- as.Date(df$Time, format = "%Y_%m_%d")
df <- df[order(df$Date), ]

expected_dates <- seq(
  as.Date("1997-01-01"),
  as.Date("2019-07-01"),
  by = "month"
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(df) == length(expected_dates),
  !anyNA(df$Date),
  all(df$Date == expected_dates),
  all(is.finite(df$ITAbond_nom)),
  all(is.finite(df$inflation)),
  all(is.finite(df$ITAbond_real)),
  all(abs(
    df$ITAbond_real -
      (df$ITAbond_nom - df$inflation)
  ) < 1e-6)
)
```

```{r yield-series, fig.cap="Monthly Italian 10-year government bond yields, January 1997–July 2019. The inflation-adjusted series subtracts contemporaneous inflation from nominal yields."}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = ITAbond_nom, color = "Nominal"),
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(
      y = ITAbond_real,
      color = "Inflation-adjusted"
    ),
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Nominal" = "#24476B",
      "Inflation-adjusted" = "#B36B35"
    ),
    breaks = c("Nominal", "Inflation-adjusted"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "5 years",
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Yield (%)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```

Nominal yields display sustained periods at different levels,
including elevated observations near the beginning of the sample
and around 2011–2012, followed by lower yields in the later years.
These patterns motivate a model with persistent latent states,
although the plot alone does not establish that three distinct
regimes generate the data.

# Three-State Gaussian HMM

Let \(Y_t\) denote the nominal yield and \(S_t\) an unobserved state
taking values in \(\{1,2,3\}\). Conditional on the state sequence,
observations are independent, with

\[
Y_t \mid S_t = k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_k,\sigma_k^2).
\]

The latent process follows a first-order Markov chain with
time-invariant transition probabilities

\[
p_{ij} = \Pr(S_t=j \mid S_{t-1}=i),
\qquad \sum_{j=1}^{3}p_{ij}=1.
\]

Each state has its own mean and variance. The model contains no
explanatory variables and is estimated on the full sample using
the expectation-maximization algorithm. This is a retrospective
classification analysis, without a separate forecasting test sample.

```{r hmm-fit, include=FALSE}
set.seed(123)

hmm_model <- depmix(
  ITAbond_nom ~ 1,
  data = df,
  nstates = 3,
  family = gaussian()
)

hmm_fit <- fit(hmm_model, verbose = FALSE)
```

State labels are arbitrary during estimation. For presentation,
we order states by increasing estimated mean yield and refer to
them as low-, medium-, and high-yield states. Numerical estimation
can converge to a local likelihood maximum.

# Parameter Estimates and Uncertainty

States are ordered by increasing estimated nominal yield.
The standard deviations below describe within-state dispersion;
they are not standard errors of the parameter estimates.

```{r extract-parameters, include=FALSE}
parameters <- getpars(hmm_fit)

initial_raw <- parameters[1:3]

transition_raw <- matrix(
  parameters[4:12],
  nrow = 3,
  byrow = TRUE
)

means_raw <- parameters[c(13, 15, 17)]
sds_raw <- parameters[c(14, 16, 18)]

state_order <- order(means_raw)

state_means <- means_raw[state_order]
state_sds <- sds_raw[state_order]
initial_probs <- initial_raw[state_order]
transition_matrix <- transition_raw[
  state_order, state_order
]

state_labels <- c(
  "Low-yield", "Medium-yield", "High-yield"
)

stopifnot(
  length(parameters) == 18L,
  all(is.finite(parameters)),
  all(state_sds > 0),
  all(transition_matrix >= -1e-8),
  all(transition_matrix <= 1 + 1e-8),
  all(abs(rowSums(transition_matrix) - 1) < 1e-6),
  abs(sum(initial_probs) - 1) < 1e-6
)
```

```{r emission-table}
emission_table <- data.frame(
  State = state_labels,
  Mean = state_means,
  SD = state_sds
)

knitr::kable(
  emission_table,
  col.names = c(
    "State", "Mean yield (%)", "SD (percentage points)"
  ),
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Estimated Gaussian emission parameters."
)
```

The transition matrix reports the probability of moving from
the state in each row to the state in each column in one month.

```{r transition-table}
dimnames(transition_matrix) <- list(
  state_labels, state_labels
)

knitr::kable(
  transition_matrix,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Estimated monthly transition probabilities."
)
```

```{r initial-probabilities-table}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    State = state_labels,
    Probability = initial_probs
  ),
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Estimated initial-state probabilities."
)
```
Estimated mean yields are 2.137%, 4.251%, and 5.639% across the
three states. Within-state dispersion is greatest in the high-yield
state and smallest in the medium-yield state.

The diagonal transition probabilities indicate high persistence
under the fitted model. However, the decoded sequence contains
few state changes, and the low-yield state appears in a single
spell extending to the end of the sample, with no observed exit
in the decoded path. This limited transition information helps
explain why its estimated self-transition probability rounds
to 1.000; it does not establish a permanently absorbing
economic regime.

The estimated initial distribution places essentially all probability
on the high-yield state. With only one observed time series,
information about the initial distribution is limited. This estimate
describes the beginning of this sequence and should not be interpreted
as the long-run distribution of states.
Approximate standard errors are computed from the numerical
observed-information matrix, accounting for the model constraints.
Parameters on or near their boundaries are excluded from this
calculation. Reported uncertainty is therefore conditional on
those boundary parameters.

```{r parameter-standard-errors}
se_output <- standardError(hmm_fit)

transition_indices <- matrix(
  4:12, nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE
)

ordered_indices <- c(
  state_order,
  as.vector(t(
    transition_indices[state_order, state_order]
  )),
  as.vector(rbind(
    12 + 2 * state_order - 1,
    12 + 2 * state_order
  ))
)

parameter_labels <- c(
  paste("Initial:", state_labels),
  unlist(lapply(state_labels, function(from) {
    paste(from, "to", state_labels)
  })),
  unlist(lapply(state_labels, function(state) {
    paste(state, c("mean", "SD"))
  }))
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(se_output) == length(parameters),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    as.numeric(se_output[[1]]),
    as.numeric(parameters),
    check.attributes = FALSE
  ))
)

uncertainty_table <- data.frame(
  Parameter = parameter_labels,
  Estimate = parameters[ordered_indices],
  SE = se_output$se[ordered_indices]
)

knitr::kable(
  uncertainty_table,
  digits = 4,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Parameter estimates and approximate standard errors."
)
```

NA denotes an unavailable standard error, not a zero standard error.
Boundary estimates limit the usual normal approximation and
require cautious interpretation.
Standard errors for the state means are 0.0740, 0.0376, and
0.0923 percentage points for the low-, medium-, and high-yield
states, respectively. Several transition probabilities have
substantial uncertainty relative to their estimates, so individual
transition patterns should be interpreted cautiously.

# State Decoding

The Viterbi algorithm identifies the most probable joint state
sequence conditional on all observations and the fitted parameters.
This is a retrospective classification, rather than a real-time
signal.

We compare observed yields with the estimated mean associated
with each decoded state.

```{r state-decoding, include=FALSE}
decoded_raw <- posterior(hmm_fit, type = "global")

state_mapping <- integer(3)
state_mapping[state_order] <- seq_len(3)

df$state <- state_mapping[decoded_raw]
df$state_mean <- state_means[df$state]

stopifnot(
  length(decoded_raw) == nrow(df),
  all(df$state %in% 1:3)
)

# Combine consecutive months assigned to the same state.
state_runs <- rle(df$state)
run_ends <- cumsum(state_runs$lengths)
run_starts <- c(1L, head(run_ends, -1L) + 1L)

month_boundaries <- c(
  df$Date,
  seq(tail(df$Date, 1), by = "month", length.out = 2)[2]
)

regime_intervals <- data.frame(
  start = month_boundaries[run_starts],
  end = month_boundaries[run_ends + 1L],
  state = factor(
    state_runs$values,
    levels = 1:3,
    labels = state_labels
  )
)
```

```{r decoded-state-plot, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Observed nominal yields and estimated means along the Viterbi-decoded state sequence. Shading identifies low-, medium-, and high-yield states. The step line represents decoded state means, not one-step-ahead forecasts."}
ggplot() +
  geom_rect(
    data = regime_intervals,
    aes(
      xmin = start,
      xmax = end,
      ymin = -Inf,
      ymax = Inf,
      fill = state
    ),
    alpha = 0.16
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = df,
    aes(x = Date, y = ITAbond_nom),
    color = "#555555",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_step(
    data = df,
    aes(x = Date, y = state_mean),
    color = "#24476B",
    linewidth = 0.55
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Low-yield" = "#579D90",
      "Medium-yield" = "#D6A756",
      "High-yield" = "#B96B64"
    ),
    drop = FALSE,
    name = "State"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "5 years",
    date_labels = "%Y",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Nominal yield (%)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```
The high-yield state appears near the beginning of the sample,
around 2000–2002, and during 2011–2012. The medium-yield state
covers much of the intervening period, while the low-yield state
dominates from approximately 2014 onward.

The decoded means summarize persistent level differences while
leaving substantial within-state fluctuations. These assignments
depend on the fitted model and do not independently identify
economic crises or structural breaks.

# Discussion and Limitations

The three-state Gaussian HMM summarizes nominal Italian bond yields
through states with different means, dispersions, and high estimated
persistence. The decoded sequence distinguishes sustained periods
of low, medium, and high yields.

The number of states is fixed at three, and transition probabilities
are assumed constant over time. The model assumes conditional
independence of observations given the state sequence; persistent
within-state dynamics could limit its adequacy and the reliability
of model-based standard errors. Estimation uses a single
initialization, so a global likelihood maximum is not established.
Boundary probability estimates also limit standard-error inference.

The analysis uses the full sample for estimation and decoding.
It therefore provides a retrospective description, without
establishing real-time classification or forecasting performance.
